name: Person Raising Hand
baseMeaning: A drawing of a figure with one arm raised high and an open hand, used as volunteering, asking to speak, or claiming the win.
tldr: 🙋 Person Raising Hand: volunteering, asking to speak, or claiming the win.

contextMeanings.meaning: The plain reading: a figure with one arm raised high and an open hand. Nothing hidden in the drawing itself.
contextMeanings.example: Claiming a task before anyone else volunteers 🙋

contextMeanings.meaning: Borrowed as a reaction, it reads as volunteering, asking to speak, or claiming the win.

contextMeanings.meaning: In a dating thread the gesture is usually doing the work of a line that was not typed. It arrives as volunteering, asking to speak, or claiming the win, softened by whatever sentence sits next to it.

In a work channel it is read the same way it is read anywhere else — volunteering, asking to speak, or claiming the win — but the stakes of a misread are higher, because the sender is often talking about somebody's actual work.

platformNotes.note: On iOS the Person Raising Hand 🙋 renders as the neutral drawing, and the neutral swatch is what most people send without thinking about it. A message like claiming a task before anyone else volunteers is the kind that carries it — the picture lands before the sentence does.

WhatsApp renders 🙋 exactly as the phone system does, but the keyboard keeps it in the gesture section, where nobody looks unless they are hunting for it. In family threads it tends to accompany a message like answering a question with a raised hand.

On Instagram 🙋 usually arrives as the tail of a caption rather than as a post of its own — a sign-off that reads as volunteering, asking to speak, or claiming the win under a photo, or a reaction somebody left on a story.

In TikTok comments 🙋 is the fastest way to answer a video without typing anything. The gesture stays volunteering, asking to speak, or claiming the win, and the tone of the comment underneath it carries the rest.

In Slack 🙋 lands in channels where the sentence was supposed to be shorter. It is usually standing in for claiming a task before anyone else volunteers, and a channel where the topic is somebody's workload is where it misreads.

generationalNotes.note: Gen Z reaches for 🙋 to do the work of claiming a task before anyone else volunteers, and treats the neutral drawing as the default rather than as a choice. What they hear first is volunteering, asking to speak, or claiming the win.

Millennials tend to send 🙋 deliberately, usually for something like answering a question with a raised hand, and they read volunteering, asking to speak, or claiming the win into it more often than the older cohorts do.
Gen X mostly uses 🙋 literally, as the picture of the gesture itself, and is less likely to read volunteering, asking to speak, or claiming the win into it than younger senders are.
Older senders use 🙋 in the most straightforward way, on family and group messages, and are less likely to hear the volunteering, asking to speak, or claiming the win subtext in it.

seoTitle: 🙋 Person Raising Hand Emoji Meaning - What Does 🙋 Really Mean?
seoDescription: What the person raising hand emoji 🙋 means in text: volunteering, asking to speak, or claiming the win. Includes the misread it invites (read as a request for attention in a meeting when it is more often playful claiming in chat, so the raised hand marks eagerness rather than politeness) and how to reply.

longForm.overview:
🙋 is the person raising hand: a figure with one arm raised high and an open hand. It arrived in Unicode 6.0, and it lives in the gesture part of the emoji set, where the drawing is doing one specific job. Somebody sends it, and the picture either stands in for a sentence or stands in for a mood. Which one it is depends on what is around it.

At the plain level the gesture reads as volunteering, asking to speak, or claiming the win. That is the reading most people arrive with, and it is usually the intended one. The picture is doing the same work as the sentence it replaces, which is why it lands faster than a sentence would have landed.

The complication is that the drawing invites a second reading. It gets read as a request for attention in a meeting when it is more often playful claiming in chat, so the raised hand marks eagerness rather than politeness. In practice that second reading is not rare — it is the one that decides how a message lands, because the sender has usually not thought about it at all.

It also sits in the crowded part of the picker. The nearest neighbour is ✋ Raised Hand: the raised hand is a stop or high-five signal, the full figure means volunteering and asking. The two are close enough that a fast thumb picks the wrong one, and the message goes out carrying a meaning nobody chose.

The drawing on this page is the neutral one. The same person raising hand exists in five skin tones, and each of those pages covers how a particular tone gets read by the people who send it. The gesture does not change between them; what changes is who it looks like it is coming from.

Practically, this is what the page is for: what the person raising hand emoji is used for, how it behaves in the places people actually use it, and where the drawing is more confident than the person who sent it. The two jobs it does most often are claiming a task before anyone else volunteers and answering a question with a raised hand, and the sections below break both of them down.
longForm.howPeopleUseIt:
The first job 🙋 does is claiming a task before anyone else volunteers. It gets typed at the end of a sentence that already made the point, and it removes the need to explain how the sender wants the message taken. Nobody has to write "you know what I mean", because the picture says it.

The second is answering a question with a raised hand. Here the emoji is doing something different: it is not the punchline, it is the tone. The message could have been sent without it, but it would have read as flat.

Where the gesture lands depends on the room. In a family thread 🙋 is closer to a sign-off, in a work channel it is a decision or a handover, and in a dating thread it is a way of making a small joke without writing one. The same drawing moves because the people reading it expect different things.

That is also why the skin-tone versions matter. The five variants under this family cover the same gesture, and the tone you pick says something about you before the sentence is read.

The habit worth naming is the one where the emoji replaces a reply altogether. Somebody asks a question, and 🙋 goes back on its own. It reads as "volunteering, asking to speak, or claiming the win", and it saves the sender a sentence — which is exactly why it is so easy to send something that means less than intended.
longForm.whenNotToUse:
Do not use 🙋 when you mean ✋ Raised Hand. The raised hand is a stop or high-five signal, the full figure means volunteering and asking. The two drawings are easy to confuse, and the wrong one changes the message from one thing to a different thing entirely.

And do not use it as a reaction to somebody who is upset. A bare 🙋 in a thread about a person reads as "volunteering, asking to speak, or claiming the win", which is about the picture and not about them.

Skip it when the sentence underneath it is the important part. The emoji gets read as a request for attention in a meeting when it is more often playful claiming in chat, so the raised hand marks eagerness rather than politeness. Once that happens the emoji is carrying the message, and the message has drifted somewhere neither sender intended.

It is also a poor choice in a first exchange with somebody you do not know. There is no warmth baked into the drawing, and person raising hand gestures often collect a slightly superior edge from being used as answers to other people's messages.

Finally, leave it out of formal settings where the tone is supposed to be neutral. 🙋 in a thread about somebody's performance, or in a message to a client you have never met, buys very little and risks a read of volunteering, asking to speak, or claiming the win as arrogance.
longForm.howToReply:
The easy reply is to match it with the same 🙋. That confirms the tone without adding anything, and it works when the original message was a reaction rather than a question.

If the person raising hand was aimed at you — a nudge, a handover, a request for a decision — answer in words. A gesture answering a gesture leaves the actual point unanswered.

If somebody sends it and you are not sure what register they are in, respond to the sentence rather than to the emoji. The drawing gets read as a request for attention in a meeting when it is more often playful claiming in chat, so the raised hand marks eagerness rather than politeness — and the sentence is the part that tells you which reading you are dealing with.

And when you want the warmth without the ambiguity, add a line of text. A message like claiming a task before anyone else volunteers almost always needs the sentence, because the picture on its own leaves the reader to guess whether you meant volunteering, asking to speak, or claiming the win or something sharper.

faqs.question: What does 🙋 mean in text?
faqs.answer: 🙋 is used for volunteering, asking to speak, or claiming the win. The drawing shows a figure with one arm raised high and an open hand, and that part is not in dispute — what changes is whether the sender is being literal or borrowing the gesture for a reaction.

faqs.question: What is the difference between 🙋 and ✋?
faqs.answer: The raised hand is a stop or high-five signal, the full figure means volunteering and asking. The two sit close together in most pickers, so the difference is often about which one the sender pressed rather than about what they meant.

faqs.question: Is 🙋 rude?
faqs.answer: It can be. The gesture is meant as volunteering, asking to speak, or claiming the win, but it gets read as a request for attention in a meeting when it is more often playful claiming in chat, so the raised hand marks eagerness rather than politeness. The risk is highest when it is the only message in the thread — a sentence gives the picture some context to sit in.

faqs.question: What does 🙋 mean from a guy?
faqs.answer: Nothing gender-specific. The same reading applies whoever sends it, and the meaning is set by the thread and by what is written next to it rather than by the sender.

faqs.question: What is the difference between 🙋 and its skin-tone versions?
faqs.answer: The tone variants under person raising hand show the same gesture in five different skin tones. The gesture does not change, but the tone is a small signal about who the sender imagines the reader is, and in some groups that signal is read louder than the sentence.

conversationExamples.message: answering a question with a raised hand 🙋
conversationExamples.interpretation: A handover or a sign-off in a channel. It reads as volunteering, asking to speak, or claiming the win, and naming the next step in words is usually clearer than leaving it to the gesture.

It gets read as a request for attention in a meeting when it is more often playful claiming in chat, so the raised hand marks eagerness rather than politeness more easily here than it does in a work thread, because the thread is thinner.
